method: The conversion treats Bloom strength as setting power per gram. A sheet of mass w grams at Bloom B carries w times B bloom-grams, and the same setting power from powder at Bloom P needs w times B divided by P grams. Bronze, silver, gold and platinum sheets are taken as 2.5 g at 140 Bloom, 2.5 g at 160 Bloom, 2.0 g at 200 Bloom and 1.7 g at 250 Bloom; a custom grade takes 0.5 to 10 g per sheet and 50 to 400 Bloom from the fields. Powdered gelatin's Bloom strength is entered directly and runs from 50 to 400. Sheet counts run from 0.5 to 200 and powder weights from 0.1 to 1000 g, with at most three decimal places and no exponent or sign notation; blank, out-of-range and malformed values are refused with a field-specific message. A conversion is refused when it would exceed 1000 g of powder or 200 sheets. Bloom-grams, grams and the 200 Bloom reference are rounded half away from zero to two decimals and sheet counts to three. Converting powder back to sheets reports the exact fractional sheet count and the percentage by which rounding to whole sheets changes the setting strength. The bloom-gram identity is linear and approximate: Bloom is measured on a 6.67 percent gel at 10 degrees Celsius, and real gels, soaking and melting losses, and differences between makers are ignored. The tool converts quantities only; it does not set a recipe's gel strength and gives no food-safety guidance. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Gelatin Manufacturers Institute of America, Gelatin Handbook: Bloom value is the force in grams needed to depress a standard gel by 4 mm, measured on a 6.67 percent gel at 10 degrees Celsius.
